strengths: The paper establishes a clean approximation-theoretic separation (poly(log log(1/ε)) vs Ω(log(1/ε)) size) between rational-activation and smooth-activation networks, and the proofs are constructive and largely self-contained (Appendices A–B build tanh, log, and sqrt blocks via Zolotarev/AGM/Halley iterations with classical capacity-based lower bounds via Gonchar).

The core constructions are numerically validated: Figure 6 verifies the doubly exponential convergence rates of the pth-root, AGM-theta, and Halley blocks against theoretical predictions, which strengthens confidence in the constructive arguments.

The theoretical analysis is complemented by a genuinely useful practical finding: the formalization in Appendix D of how normalization layers create non-identifiability and gradient amplification for adaptive rational activations, and the empirical demonstration (Tables 2 and 5) that GroupNorm/LayerNorm disproportionately hurts rational variants while normalization-free ViT fails for fixed activations but succeeds with rationals.

The empirical evaluation spans three distinct domains (CIFAR-10 with VGG, offline MuJoCo RL with IQL and TD3+BC, and Tiny ImageNet with ViT/CaiT/Swin) under controlled activation-only changes, with five seeds, mean±std reporting, learning curves, and detailed hyperparameter tables (Tables 6–10), supporting reproducibility.

The limitations section is honest and specific: it acknowledges small-to-mid scale, single-GPU constraints, limited seed sweeps, and that wall-clock timings are confounded by implementation overhead; the paper also candidly notes (Section 4.1) that learned rational activations operate mostly in smooth regions, i.e., the practical gains are not fully explained by the kink-approximation theory.
weaknesses: The headline separation has an asymmetry in assumptions that weakens the main claim: the Ω(log(1/ε)) lower bound for GELU networks (Theorem 3.2 / B.2) applies only to networks with uniformly bounded weights and biases, while the rational-network upper bounds do not appear to be subject to an analogous constraint. Since practical networks have unbounded weights, the claimed exponential parameter-efficiency advantage over smooth activations is established only for a restricted smooth-network class; the paper does not clearly flag this caveat in the main text.

The theoretical novelty is incremental relative to Boulé et al. (2020): the log–log vs log separation mechanism, the degree-based bounds on rational networks, and the composition/propagation argument in Theorem C.1 are direct extensions of the established rational-vs-ReLU analysis to smooth activations (essentially by composing known tanh/exp/log approximations). The transformer and gated-activation extensions (Section 3.4) are informal discussions rather than proved theorems.

There is a disconnect between the theory and the experiments: the expressivity advantage is proven for targets with kinks or nearby singularities, yet the paper's own activation-shape diagnostics (Figures 2, 4, 9–13) show that learned rationals are evaluated in smooth, slowly varying regions. The empirical gains (roughly 1–3 points on CIFAR-10, moderate RL improvements largely consistent with prior work such as Delfosse et al. 2024) are therefore not strongly attributable to the proven separations, and the paper concedes this.

Experimental scale and statistical power are limited: VGG4/VGG8 on CIFAR-10, 300K-update offline RL on three MuJoCo-medium tasks, and Tiny ImageNet with three transformer families, all with five seeds on a single consumer GPU. Several results (e.g., Swin-T in Table 5, HalfCheetah with TD3+BC in Table 4) are within noise of the baselines, and no significance testing is provided.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: the limitations section states all experiments ran on an RTX 4090 laptop while the Software and Data section states an RTX 4070; the theory targets the tanh-approximate GELU rather than the erf-GELU actually used in modern architectures without clearly delimiting the gap; Theorem A.1 is referenced where Lemma A.1 is defined, and Theorems B.1/A.2/A.3 in the proofs correspond to Lemmas B.1/A.2/A.3; the GitHub URL in the Software and Data section is incomplete (ends at 'github.com/'), which undermines the reproducibility claim.

The contribution framing overstates practical reach: the claim that rational activations 'could form a foundation for deep learning architectures' is not supported at any realistic scale, and the normalization analysis (Appendix D) is qualitative (gradient bounds and invariance directions) rather than yielding actionable stabilization methods.

strengths: The constructive proofs in the appendices are careful and elegant: the pth-root recursion (Gawlik & Nakatsukasa), the AGM-theta logarithm construction (Sasaki-Kanada), and the Halley-based tanh block compose into a clean O(log^3 log(1/eps)) upper bound for approximating GELU, and Figure 6 numerically verifies the claimed doubly-exponential convergence rates of the core blocks.

The paper usefully formalizes an underexplored practical issue: the interaction between trainable rational activations and normalization layers, including an explicit non-identifiability/invariance analysis (Eq. 19-21) and coefficient-sensitivity bounds (Appendix D). This is a genuine, if specialized, contribution that explains the observed GroupNorm/LayerNorm degradations.

The empirical protocol is mostly transparent: hyperparameter tables, seeds, evaluation details, and learned-activation-shape diagnostics are provided, and the limitations section candidly acknowledges the small scale (single laptop GPU, no LLM-scale runs).
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty. The core log log(1/eps) vs. log(1/eps) separation is already established in Boullé et al. (2020) for ReLU; the paper's contribution is essentially transplanting this to GELU-family activations via classical singularity/condenser-capacity arguments (Theorem A.4) and known rational-approximation machinery. The converse direction is also not tight (O(log^2) upper bound vs. Omega(log) lower bound in Thms 3.2/3.3), weakening the claimed 'exponential gap' narrative, and all lower bounds critically assume uniformly bounded parameters — a restriction that disconnects the theory from the unbounded-parameter networks actually trained in the experiments.

The theory-practice link is admitted to be weak by the authors themselves: Section 4.1 states the learned rational activations 'are evaluated mostly in regions where the rationals are smooth and slowly varying, so they are not being used to approximate kinks or high curvature.' The expressivity mechanism that motivates the paper is thus not the one producing the (modest) empirical gains, which undercuts the paper's central framing.

Experimental evidence is limited and partly unconvincing: only VGG4/VGG8 on CIFAR-10, three MuJoCo-medium tasks, and Tiny ImageNet. Gains are modest (roughly 1-2 points on VGG, under a point on Swin-T where GELU actually wins, and mixed on ViT/CaiT). Under GroupNorm on VGG8, rationals lose to GELU (91.80/92.13 vs. 92.21), so the headline 'match or outperform' claim does not uniformly hold.

Questionable evaluation protocol: Tables 1-3 and 5 report 'best test accuracy over training' (test-set peeking), and Table 2 reports the better of two initialization settings per activation, introducing selection bias in favor of whichever variant does best on the test set. This inflates apparent gains relative to an honest final-epoch or validation-selected protocol.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code URL in the Software and Data section is truncated ('https://github.com/' with no repository path), and there is an internal inconsistency about the hardware (RTX 4090 in Section 5 vs. RTX 4070 in the Software section), which casts doubt on the accuracy of the experimental reporting.

Presentation sloppiness: listing Softmax/LogSoftmax as 'activation functions' in the abstract, dangling lemma/theorem cross-references (Theorem A.1/A.2/A.3 cited where Lemma A.1/A.2/A.3 are proven; 'Theorem B.1' where Lemma B.1 is stated), typos ('augemented', 'with away from poles away from'), and loosely dated references (e.g., Vaswani et al. 2023, Hendrycks & Gimpel 2023) suggest the manuscript was not carefully finalized.

The normalization-free ViT result (61.24 while ReLU/GELU 'failed') is presented as a headline success but is the least-controlled experiment: a single configuration where baselines diverge, omitting variance/seed detail, and driven by a separate mechanism (Zhu et al. 2025) rather than the paper's expressivity theory.

strengths: The paper provides a clean and carefully executed extension of the rational-vs-ReLU separations of Boulé et al. (2020) to the family of smooth activations actually used in modern architectures (GELU, SiLU, ELU, etc.), including gated variants and transformer-style MLP blocks — a relevant and previously unaddressed setting.

The proofs are constructive and grounded in classical approximation theory (Zolotarev/AGM–theta logarithm constructions, Halley iteration, Bernstein ellipses, condenser capacity), and the convergence behavior of the core building blocks is numerically verified (Figure 6), which increases confidence in the constructions.

The experimental program is unusually thorough for the claimed compute budget: controlled activation swaps across VGGs on CIFAR-10, three transformer families on Tiny ImageNet, and two offline RL algorithms on MuJoCo, with fixed architectures/optimizers, five seeds, and honest reporting of cases where rationals do not win (e.g., GroupNorm interactions, Swin-T).

The analysis of normalization–adaptive-activation interference (Appendix D: affine reparameterization non-identifiability and coefficient-gradient amplification) is a genuinely interesting and testable side contribution that explains an observed empirical phenomenon.

The limitations section is candid and specific (single-GPU scale, non-fused kernels, no LLM-scale evaluation), and the authors openly note that the learned rationals are not exploiting the kink-approximation regime their theory predicts, which is an honest connection between theory and practice.
weaknesses: The headline 'exponential separation' claims hold only under a uniform boundedness assumption on the smooth network's weights and biases. This is a substantive restriction: unbounded weights (standard in practice) can in principle generate the required curvature, so the Ω(log(1/ε)) lower bounds (Theorems 3.2, 3.4 part 2) do not rule out efficient unbounded-parameter GELU approximations. The paper states the assumption but the abstract/introduction do not adequately qualify the central claim.

The 'size' metric is ambiguous and inconsistently used (the Appendix A lower bound derives constraints on W³L and then quotes WL = Ω(log log(1/ε)), while parameter counts scale like W²L); this should be made precise, as it affects the strength of the stated lower bounds.

The upper and lower bounds do not match (O(log³log(1/ε)) vs Ω(log log(1/ε)) for rational approximation of GELU; O(log²) vs Ω(log) in the converse direction), so the separations are qualitative rather than sharp.

The theory–practice link is loose: the theory concerns targets with singularities/nearby poles, but the authors' own diagnostic (Section 4.1, Figure 2) shows the learned activations operate in smooth, slowly varying regions. Thus the empirical gains, while consistent, are not explained by the approximation-theoretic separation, weakening the paper's narrative.

Reproducibility is undermined by sloppiness: the public code URL in 'Software and Data' is incomplete ('https://github.com/' with no repository path), and the hardware is inconsistently reported (RTX 4090 in Section 5 vs RTX 4070 in the Software and Data section), which casts doubt on the provenance of the reported runs.

The Tiny ImageNet 'no norm' comparison reports fixed-activation runs as 'failed' and omits them from the accuracy summary; while the protocol is described, the headline 'large gain' claim rests on an asymmetric comparison with no successful fixed-activation baseline.

The contribution is incremental relative to Boulé et al. (2020): the separation mechanism (rational functions efficiently encode nearby singularities) is known; the novelty is the transfer to smooth activations, which is useful but not conceptually surprising.
Minor presentation issues ('augemented', Lemma/Theorem label inconsistencies, the erf-GELU vs tanh-GELU discrepancy is not clearly flagged) suggest the manuscript needed one more careful pass.

strengths: The main theoretical contribution is clean and well-motivated: an exponential separation in parameter complexity between rational and smooth-activation networks (log-log vs. log scaling in 1/ε), extending the ReLU-vs-rational separation of Boulle et al. (2020) to the smooth activations actually used in modern architectures (GELU, Swish/SiLU, Mish, ELU-family, etc.), and lifting scalar results to full networks (Theorem 4.4/Appendix C) and to gated/transformer settings.

The constructive upper-bound proofs are unusually complete and verifiable: the appendix assembles a pth-root block (following Gawlik & Nakatsukasa), an AGM-theta logarithm block (Sasaki–Kanada), an artanh block, and a Halley-based tanh block, with careful tracking of error accumulation under inexact inner blocks; the numerical verification of doubly exponential convergence rates (Figure 5) is a nice touch.

Lower bounds are grounded in classical approximation theory (condenser capacity via Gonchar for the rational side; a finite-difference curvature argument for the smooth side with uniformly bounded parameters), and the curvature-based family r_eta(x) = eta^2/(x^2+eta^2) gives an intuitive witness for the Ω(log(1/ε)) barrier.

The paper makes a genuinely useful practical observation: normalization layers interact badly with adaptive rational activations (non-identifiability from absorbable affine reparameterization, plus gradient-noise amplification from polynomial coefficient sensitivities), formalized in Appendix D and corroborated experimentally (GroupNorm drops for rationals in Table 2; the normalization-free ViT result in Table 5).

Experiments cover three distinct domains (CIFAR-10 with VGG, offline RL with IQL/TD3+BC on MuJoCo medium, Tiny ImageNet with ViT/CaiT/Swin) under matched architectures, optimizers, and budgets, with five seeds, variance reporting, extensive hyperparameter tables, layerwise activation-shape diagnostics, and a public code link; reproducibility is treated seriously.

The limitations section is honest and specific (single RTX 4070 laptop, small-to-mid scale, no LLM-scale evaluation, implementation-dependent wall-clock timings), and the paper candidly reports settings where rationals do not lead (Swin-T) and where removing LayerNorm hurts.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is incremental relative to Boulle et al. (2020) and Telgarsky (2017): the core separation mechanism (rational functions beat ReLU-type nets by a log vs log-log factor) is known, and the main new work is assembling constructions that carry it to GELU-style smooth activations. The lower-bound side relies on a bounded-parameter assumption whose connection to trained networks is loose; the headline 'exponentially more expressive' claim applies to worst-case rational targets with nearby poles, not to the analytic smooth targets that dominate in practice.

There is a visible theory-practice disconnect that the paper itself concedes: the learned rational activations operate in smooth, slowly varying regions and are 'not being used to approximate kinks or high curvature,' so the approximation-theoretic separation does not directly explain the empirical gains. The mechanism behind the observed improvements (initialization to LeakyReLU/GELU shapes, adaptive shaping) is left largely unexplained.

Experimental scale and strength of evidence are modest: all results come from a single consumer laptop, sample sizes are small (five seeds, no statistical significance testing), reporting 'best value over training' slightly inflates comparisons, and transformer gains are marginal or within noise except for CaiT-S24 and the no-norm ViT setting; baseline variances in offline RL (e.g., Walker2d ±11.5) are large relative to the reported margins in some settings.

Several claims are stated more broadly than the proofs support: the Ω(log(1/ε)) smooth-side lower bound requires uniformly bounded weights/biases and depth-bounded derivative growth, but this restriction is easy to miss in the abstract and introduction; similarly, statements covering Softmin/Softmax/LogSoftmax in the activation list are not individually verified in detail (the appendix argues by representation, with GELU as the 'representative' case).

Minor presentation issues: occasional typos and awkward phrasing ('we will we refer to'), the claim that normalization 'is intrinsically disadvantageous' is stronger than the analysis warrants (it identifies mechanisms, not a lower bound on training performance), and the extension to transformers (Section 4.4) is essentially an argument by substitution rather than a new theorem.

The practical recommendation surface is narrow: runtime overhead is consistently positive (52–77 vs 50–56 units in tables, unfused implementation), and the paper does not establish where the parameter-efficiency advantage would matter at the scales where it predicts the biggest gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a question of genuine interest—whether trainable rational activations offer provable expressivity advantages over modern smooth activations—and delivers real, non-trivial approximation-theoretic content, including an elaborate constructive proof (p-th root iteration, AGM–theta logarithm, Halley-based tanh construction) with numerical verification of the doubly exponential convergence rates (Figure 5).

The separation results are broad: the log–log vs. log parameter scaling is shown for a large family of transcendental activations (GELU, SiLU, ELU, Mish, Softplus, etc.), extended to gated activations, and lifted to full feedforward architectures (Theorems 4.1–4.4).

The analysis of normalization–adaptive-activation interactions (Section 4.5, Appendix D), including the non-identifiability/invariance mechanism and coefficient-gradient bounds, is a novel and practically relevant observation.

The experimental section covers three distinct domains (CIFAR-10 VGGs, offline MuJoCo RL with IQL/TD3+BC, Tiny ImageNet transformers) with five seeds, learning curves, layerwise activation visualizations, and unusually detailed reproducibility tables (Tables 6–10).
The limitations section is honest and specific about scale (single RTX 4070 laptop), missing sweeps, and implementation-dependent wall-clock timings.
weaknesses: The central headline claim—that rational networks are 'exponentially more expressive' than smooth-activation networks—rests on an asymmetric and somewhat artificial setup: the Ω(log(1/ε)) lower bounds (Theorems 4.2, B.2, 4.4) hold only for networks with uniformly bounded weights/biases, while the rational side carries no comparable restriction. GELU/SiLU networks with unbounded weights are universal approximators and can realize sharp features with large weights, so the separation is about bounded-parameter smooth networks, which should be foregrounded much more prominently than it is.

There is a serious disconnect between the theory and the empirics: the theory's advantage mechanism requires targets with kinks or nearby complex singularities, yet the paper itself concedes (Section 5.1) that learned rational activations 'are evaluated mostly in regions where the rationals are smooth and slowly varying, so they are not being used to approximate kinks or high curvature.' The empirical gains therefore cannot be attributed to the proven separation, weakening the paper's narrative coherence.

Several lower-bound derivations are sketchy. In Appendix A, the final step asserting 'the minimum value of WL (the number of parameters...) gives WL = Ω(log log(1/ε))' from the constraint C·W³L ≥ log(1/ε) does not follow as stated (parameter count of a width-W, depth-L network does not scale as WL, and the minimization over W is not carried out); the reasoning that W^{3L} is intended, and the size definition (units vs. parameters), needs to be made precise. Similar 'standard stability argument' hand-waves appear in Lemma A.2/A.3 for the error accumulation under inexact artanh substitution in a cubically convergent iteration.

The empirical protocol contains selection and fairness concerns: Table 1 reports 'best value over training' on the test set; the augmented pipeline reports the better of two initialization toggles per activation; and rational coefficients receive model-specific learning-rate multipliers (2/4/8 in Table 10) that fixed activations do not receive, confounding the activation comparison—particularly in the no-normalization ViT result where baselines diverge to NaN and the rational model is effectively serving as an additional learned normalization mechanism rather than demonstrating expressivity.

The experimental scale is small (VGG4/8 on CIFAR-10, 100-epoch Tiny ImageNet, three MuJoCo medium tasks), with large baseline variances in the RL tables (e.g., GELU ±10.77, Rational ±11.52 on Walker2d), so several headline gaps are within roughly one to two standard deviations; no significance testing is provided.

The transformer extension (Section 4.4) is informal—the claim that the scalar separation 'is expected to preserve the advantage' for transformers is an assertion, not a theorem—yet it is counted among the contributions.
Reproducibility is undermined by the code link being empty in the manuscript ('Code is available at' with no URL), despite the claim of availability.

The theoretical contribution is incremental relative to Boulé et al. (2020), which already established the log–log vs. log rational/ReLU separation; the novelty here is extending it to smooth activations, which is valuable but unlikely to change practice, and the writing occasionally oversells (e.g., 'rational activations could form a mathematically natural and computationally efficient foundation for deep learning architectures').

strengths: The paper delivers a coherent theory-practice package: constructive approximation-theoretic separations between rational and smooth-activation networks, backed by empirical evaluation across vision (CIFAR-10 with VGG, Tiny ImageNet with ViT/CaiT/Swin), and offline RL (IQL, TD3+BC on MuJoCo medium tasks).

The constructive proofs are technically substantive: the GELU construction chains p-th root, AGM-theta logarithm, artanh, and Halley-based tanh blocks with careful error propagation to obtain the O((log log(1/ε))^3) upper bound, and the lower bound (Theorem A.4) is grounded in classical condenser-capacity results for rational approximation (Gonchar; Saff & Totik). The numerical verification of doubly-exponential convergence rates (Figure 5) is a nice touch.

The extension of the log-log versus log separation beyond GELU to the broader transcendental family (ELU, SiLU, Mish, SELU, etc.), to gated activations, and to network level (Theorem 4.4) is a genuine, if incremental, advance over the ReLU-vs-rational separation of Boulé et al. (2020).

The analysis of normalization-induced conditioning issues for adaptive rationals (Appendix D: affine absorbance non-identifiability, polynomial moment amplification of gradient noise) is a concrete, falsifiable hypothesis that the CIFAR-10 GroupNorm ablations then test empirically; the NaN-divergence of fixed-activation norm-free ViT versus stable rational training is an interesting observation.

The experiments are reasonably well-controlled within blocks (fixed architecture, optimizer, budget; five seeds; mean ± std; learning curves), and hyperparameters are documented in detail (Tables 6-10).

The limitations section is candid: single RTX 4070, small-to-mid scale, no LLM-scale evaluation, wall-clock timings confounded by implementation, and the honest admission that the learned activations are evaluated mostly in smooth regions rather than near kinks.
weaknesses: The most important lower bound (Theorem 4.2 / B.2, and hence the Ω(log(1/ε)) side of the headline separation) holds only for GELU networks with uniformly bounded weights and biases, and the hard target R_ε itself depends on ε. Unbounded weights can trivially produce the required curvature, so the claimed 'exponential expressivity gap over modern smooth activations' is substantially weaker than the abstract suggests; the main text (Theorem 4.4, part 2) does not clearly restate the bounded-parameter hypothesis, which reads as a stronger claim than what is proven.

There is a disconnect between the theory and the empirical claims. The theory concerns the extreme uniform-approximation regime (ε → 0, non-smooth targets like |x| or functions with nearby complex poles), whereas the paper's own Figure 2 analysis admits that the learned rational activations operate mostly where they are smooth and 'are not being used to approximate kinks or high curvature.' The observed empirical gains therefore do not follow from, and are not explained by, the approximation-theoretic separation, even though the framing implies they do ('these gains translate into improved accuracy').

Empirical novelty is limited relative to prior work: Delfosse et al. (2024) already showed rational activations boost deep RL, and rational-activation implementations exist. No comparison against other trainable/adaptive activation baselines (e.g., Pade Activation Units, APL, or other learned nonlinearities) is provided, only fixed activations, which weakens the claim that rationals specifically are advantageous rather than 'adaptive' in general.

Potential fairness concern in the transformer experiments: rational coefficients receive model-specific learning-rate multipliers (2, 4, 8 for CaiT, ViT, Swin in Table 10) and weight decay zero, while fixed activations apparently receive no equivalent per-model tuning. The strongest result (norm-free ViT where GELU/ReLU diverge to NaN) is exactly the setting most sensitive to such tuning, so the 'rational-only' stability claim needs a more careful ablation.

Experimental scale and effect sizes are modest: most Tiny ImageNet gains (e.g., Swin-T 60.66 vs 60.76 for GELU) are within roughly one standard deviation of five seeds; several RL results have large variance (e.g., Walker2d 72.28 ± 11.52). Reporting best-over-training test accuracy (Table 1) constitutes mild selection on the test set.

The 'Software and Data' section appears to reference a code URL that is blank/incomplete in the manuscript, which undermines the reproducibility claim despite otherwise detailed hyperparameter documentation.

Presentation issues: typos and informal passages ('we will we refer', 'there's a curiosity'), and Theorem 4.1's lower bound statement ('no rational network of size o(log log(1/ε))') versus the abstract's Ω(log log(1/ε)) versus the appendix's Ω(log log(1/ε)) via W^3 L degree bounds should be stated consistently; the gap between O((log log)^3) upper and Ω(log log) lower is also not highlighted as such.

The claim that rational activations 'could form a mathematically natural and computationally efficient foundation for deep learning architectures' (Section 4.6 / contributions) is overclaimed given the bounded-parameter caveat in the theory and the single-GPU empirical scope.
